newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria to open up television and radio markets.
newsitem.headline: Austria to open up television and radio markets.

text.p: Austria, one of the last strongholds of state-controlled broadcasting, unveiled a draft law on Wednesday that will open the market to private radio and television stations and break the monopoly of state-owned ORF.
"This law is a milestone in creating a liberal environment for media. It will bring diversity and create jobs," Social Democrat Chancellor Viktor Klima told a news conference.

"The new cable and satellite television law will be the most liberal in Europe and in most cases meets the demands of the People's Party," said Vice Chancellor Wolfgang Schuessel, who leads the junior coalition partner, the conservative People's Party.
The breakthrough marked the end of years of political squabbling culminating in 1993 when the European Court of Human Rights ruled that Austrian media laws violated the right to free speech.

Austrians, unlike most of their east European neighbours, were still putting up with the choice of just two state-owned terrestrial television channels ORF 1 and ORF 2, which often broadcast the same programme simultaneously.

The arrival of cable and satellite television beaming German commercial stations RTL, SAT 1 and PRO 7 widened the selection in recent years but the domestic market remained firmly closed to private broadcasters.
Austrian radio laws were no less restrictive, with ORF running the only national stations.

Klima forecast the section of the bill governing private radio would be the first to clear parliament, allowing up to 55 newcomers to gain a licence and start broadcasting regionally and locally in the autumn of this year.
None of the planned 10 regional and 45 local stations will compete with ORF's national radio franchise, however.
Regulations allowing cable and satellite television firms to enter the domestic market will take longer to implement and are unlikely to enter the statute book before early 1998.

Cable stations will not need a licence to broadcast. The only restrictions will limit media stakes to 26 percent and foreign stakes, excluding the Europe Economic Area -- comprising European Union members and some non-EU western European countries -- to 49 percent. Political parties, communities and ORF will not be allowed to buy into private radio stations under the draft law.
The future of ORF, which is currently financed by a mix of viewer fees and advertising, remained unclear.
There were no immediate plans for a third terrestrial television station to compete with ORF 1 and ORF 2 but critics said the state channels were bound to lose ground to newcomers.

"The Social Democrats have allowed themselves to be pulled over the table by the People's Party and they have approved a law that will eventually lead to a massive concentration of the media market," said opposition Greens MP Terezija Stoisits.

The Social Democrats, traditionally allied to state broadcaster ORF, had resisted big changes to the media law. The conservative People's Party had argued in favour of lifting restrictions on private stations.
